newsitem.title: PERU: Peru searches for miners after quake kills nine.
newsitem.headline: Peru searches for miners after quake kills nine.

text.p: Rescue workers tried on Wednesday to reach remote mining villages in southern Peru where at least 13 miners were feared trapped underground after an earthquake left nine people dead and more than 500 injured.

Tens of thousands of people spent the night on the streets after their houses were destroyed by the quake, which shook southern Peru at midday on Tuesday and rocked Lima for a minute. The hardest-hit towns were along the Pacific coast: Nazca, 290 miles (460 km) south of the capital Lima, where 300 were injured, and Ica, 100 miles (160 km) farther north, where another 200 were injured, officials said on Wednesday.
Army and police flew tents, blankets and food into Nazca, where six of the deaths occurred. The quake left 25,000 homes uninhabitable, according to Mayor Luz Torres Zegarra.

Fire Chief Otacar Lucar, coordinating rescue operations from Nazca, said there were reports that 13 miners were trapped in three gold mining zones in the department of Ica at Incas, Salamarca, Ingenio.
"I ran out of the mine but my two friends ... were trapped in there," Julian Huaman, who walked 14 miles (23 km) to Nazca after escaping from the collapsing mine, told Reuters.

One miner died in Moyohauca, 375 miles (600 km) south of Lima, in the department of Arequipa and ten more were seriously injured, said Celso Cahachahua, a community leader in the mining village, without giving more details.

President Alberto Fujimori, speaking on Peruvian radio from Japan during a nine-day official visit to Asia, said early reports were false that 300 workers were trapped at the "Huanca" gold mine 310 miles (500 km) south of Lima.

"I took the decision to return when I was initially informed about 300 miners trapped in tunnels. But this news has now been discounted," Fujimori said, adding that he would continue his trip to Japan and Southeast Asia.

The quake measured 6.4 on the Richter scale and its epicentre was 65 miles (100 km) southeast of Ica, Luis Vilca of the Peruvian Geophysic Institute said. By early on Wednesday, Nazca had experienced at least 200 aftershocks, including one late Tuesday that measured 4.2 on the Richter scale, Vilca said.

Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi, the top government official in Fujimori's absence, said he was flying to mining zones, including Huanca. Most areas were cut off by road, and rain and fog seriously hampered rescue operations by air, the prime minister said.
